# How to use this guide

PHAR(II)205 Applied Pharmacology II is a Semester 4 subject of the INC 2021 B.Sc Nursing curriculum. It directly continues PHAR(I)205 from Semester 3, completing the full pharmacology course. This semester covers the remaining INC drug groups — reproductive, emergency, immunological and nutritional drugs — and concludes with the fundamental principles of prescribing that govern the nurse's professional practice.

## Exam pattern

PHAR(II)205 is **not examined in a standalone paper**. It is examined as **Section A of a combined 3-hour, 75-mark university paper** shared with Pathology II and Genetics (PATH(II)210):

| Section | Subject | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Pharmacology II (PHAR(II)205) | 38 |
| B | Pathology (Part I + Part II) | 25 |
| C | Genetics | 12 |
| **Total** | | **75** |

Confirm the exact format with your university — INC Regulations 2020, Appendix 3 sets the framework but universities print papers in slightly different styles.

**Section A pharmacology question pattern** (approximate, based on a 38-mark allocation):

| Part | Type | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2 long essays (from 3 given; answer any 2) | 10 marks each | 20 |
| Short answers (from about 9 given; answer any 7) | 5 marks each | 35 short — but this section only 18 of 35 goes to pharmacology |
| MCQs / very short answers | 1–2 marks each | Remaining |

Confirm with your college; INC examinations vary in Section C split.

## How the units are arranged

This guide has seven unit files. The numbers match the StudyDesk unit numbers:

| Notes file | INC Unit | Topics covered |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unit 1 | Pharmacology of ENT, Eye and Urinary system drugs | Decongestants, ear drops, eye drops, diuretics, urinary tract drugs |
| Unit 2 | Analgesics, antipyretics, anti-inflammatory and anaesthetic drugs | Opioids, NSAIDs, COX-2 inhibitors, local and general anaesthetics |
| Unit 3 | Psychotropic, CNS and muscle-relaxant drugs | Sedatives, anxiolytics, antidepressants, antipsychotics, anticonvulsants, CNS stimulants |
| Unit 4 | Sex hormones, contraception, uterine drugs and drugs in pregnancy | Oestrogens, progestogens, contraceptive methods, uterotonics (oxytocin, misoprostol, ergometrine), tocolytics, MgSO4, teratogens |
| Unit 5 | Emergency drugs, deaddiction, IV fluids, poisoning and nutrition | Adrenaline, atropine, inotropes, adenosine, deaddiction drugs, IV fluids, antidotes, vitamins and minerals |
| Unit 6 | Vaccines, anticancer drugs, immunomodulators and alternative medicine | National immunisation schedule, antisera, chemotherapy classes and toxicities, immunosuppressants, biologics, AYUSH |
| Unit 7 | Fundamental principles of prescribing | WHO six steps, drug schedules (India), prescriptions, medication errors, five rights, pharmacovigilance, ADR reporting, PvPI |

## Scoring tips

1. **Begin every answer with the drug class and mechanism before listing drug names.** Examiners reward organised pharmacological thinking.
2. **End every answer with 2–3 nurse's responsibilities.** INC exam questions in pharmacology almost always carry marks for nursing application.
3. **Tables earn marks quickly** — use a table for drug comparisons (oxytocin vs misoprostol vs ergometrine; OCP vs POP; types of contraception; antidotes).
4. **State adverse effects and contraindications** for every drug group — these are frequently asked.
5. **Use the class → drug → mechanism → uses → adverse effects → nurse frame** as your backbone for any long essay.
6. **Learn doses where they are clinically critical** — adrenaline 0.5 mg IM; MgSO4 4 g loading + 1–2 g/h maintenance; oxytocin 10 IU IM for PPH.

## Probability ratings

- **High** — appears in most examination papers in some form
- **Medium** — appears every few papers, or as a component of a larger question
- **Low** — less frequent but useful for MCQs

## High-probability topics by unit

| Unit | High-probability topics |
| --- | --- |
| 4 | OCP — mechanism, adverse effects, contraindications, missed pill; PPH drugs compared; magnesium sulfate — dosing, toxicity, antidote; drugs to avoid in pregnancy (teratogens) |
| 5 | Adrenaline for anaphylaxis; antidotes table (paracetamol, opioids, organophosphates, benzodiazepines); IV fluid compositions; vitamins B12, folic acid, thiamine (Wernicke's); activated charcoal |
| 6 | National immunisation schedule; cold chain; nurse's role in immunisation; anticancer drugs — classification and toxicities; nurse's role in chemotherapy; cyclosporine and tacrolimus |
| 7 | Five rights of medication administration; medication error types; ADR reporting (PvPI); drug schedules (H, H1, X); WHO prescribing steps |

# Last-night revision sheet — PHAR(II)205 Applied Pharmacology II

PHAR(II)205 is examined as **Section A (38 marks)** of the Semester 4 combined paper (Pharmacology II + Pathology + Genetics, 75 marks, 3 hours).

---

## Contraception — key facts

**OCP mechanism:** Inhibit LH/FSH → no ovulation; thicken cervical mucus → sperm blocked; thin endometrium.

**OCP absolute contraindications:** Age > 35 AND smoker; migraine WITH aura; personal history of DVT/PE; oestrogen-dependent cancer; active liver disease; breastfeeding in first 6 weeks.

**Missed OCP:** > 12 hours late → take missed pill + barrier method for 7 days.

| Method | Key point |
| --- | --- |
| COCP | Oestrogen + progestogen; CI: smoking/migraine/DVT |
| POP (minipill) | Progestogen only; 3-hour window; safe if oestrogen CI |
| Emergency — levonorgestrel | Within 72 hours; 1.5 mg oral |
| Emergency — ulipristal | Within 120 hours; 30 mg oral |
| Emergency — copper IUD | Within 120 hours; most effective |
| DMPA injection | 150 mg IM every 3 months |
| Implant | Etonogestrel; 3 years; immediate efficacy |

---

## PPH drugs

| Drug | Dose | Key caution |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Oxytocin | 10 IU IM (or IV slowly) — first line | Hyperstimulation; water intoxication at high IV doses |
| Misoprostol | 600 mcg oral/sublingual — community | Shivering and fever (expected); no refrigeration needed |
| Ergometrine | 0.5 mg IM or IV slowly | **CI in hypertension** |
| Tranexamic acid | 1 g IV within 3 hours of birth | Antifibrinolytic; adjunct |
| Syntometrine | Oxytocin 5 IU + ergometrine 0.5 mg IM | CI in hypertension |

---

## Magnesium sulfate (pre-eclampsia/eclampsia)

- **Loading:** 4 g IV over 15–20 min
- **Maintenance:** 1–2 g/h IV infusion
- **Toxicity monitoring — HOURLY:** patellar reflex (lost first) → RR < 12/min → urine < 25 mL/h
- **Antidote at the bedside:** calcium gluconate 10 mL 10% IV slowly

---

## Teratogens

| Drug | Risk |
| --- | --- |
| Sodium valproate | Neural tube defects, foetal valproate syndrome |
| Warfarin | Warfarin embryopathy; foetal haemorrhage |
| Isotretinoin (retinoids) | Severe craniofacial/cardiac/CNS malformations |
| ACE inhibitors | Foetal renal damage (2nd/3rd trimester) |
| NSAIDs (3rd trimester) | Premature closure of ductus arteriosus |
| Aminoglycosides | Foetal ototoxicity |

---

## Emergency drugs (mnemonic: AADAN)

- **A**drenaline — anaphylaxis 0.5 mg IM outer thigh; cardiac arrest 1 mg IV
- **A**tropine — bradycardia; organophosphate poisoning (large IV doses)
- **D**igoxin toxicity signs — nausea, yellow-green visual haloes, bradycardia; antidote: Digibind (Fab)
- **A**denosine — SVT conversion; 6 mg IV rapid bolus + 20 mL saline flush
- **N**oradrenaline / dopamine / dobutamine — vasopressor/inotropes in shock

---

## Antidotes (must-know table)

| Poison | Antidote |
| --- | --- |
| Paracetamol | N-acetylcysteine (NAC) — within 8 h best; use Rumack nomogram |
| Opioids | Naloxone 0.4–2 mg IV/IM/intranasal; short-acting — may need repeat |
| Benzodiazepines | Flumazenil — caution in TCA co-ingestion, dependence |
| Organophosphates | Atropine (large doses) + pralidoxime (early) |
| Iron | Desferrioxamine (urine turns pink-rose) |
| Tricyclic antidepressants | Sodium bicarbonate IV (reverses Na-channel block) |
| Digoxin (severe) | Digibind (Fab fragments) |
| Cyanide | Hydroxocobalamin IV |
| Warfarin overdose | Vitamin K1 + FFP |
| MgSO4 toxicity | Calcium gluconate 10 mL 10% IV |

---

## IV fluid compositions

| Fluid | Na+ (mmol/L) | K+ | Cl− | Other |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0.9% NaCl | 154 | 0 | 154 | — |
| Ringer's lactate | 130 | 4 | 109 | Ca2+ 2.7, lactate 28 |
| 5% Dextrose | 0 | 0 | 0 | Glucose 50 g/L |

---

## Vaccines

**Live attenuated (CI in pregnancy/immunocompromise):** BCG, MMR, OPV, Rotavirus, Varicella

**Inactivated:** IPV, Hepatitis A, Influenza

**Toxoid:** Tetanus (TT), Diphtheria (DT/Td)

**Subunit/conjugate:** Hepatitis B, HPV, Hib, PCV, Meningococcal

**Cold chain:** 2–8°C for most; OPV at −20°C.

---

## Anticancer drug toxicities

| Drug | Specific toxicity | Management |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cyclophosphamide | Haemorrhagic cystitis | MESNA + hydration |
| Methotrexate | Mucositis, hepatotoxicity | Leucovorin rescue |
| Doxorubicin | Cardiomyopathy (cumulative) | Echo monitoring; dose limit |
| Bleomycin | Pulmonary fibrosis | PFTs; minimise oxygen |
| Vincristine | Peripheral neuropathy | No IM injections; never intrathecal |
| Cisplatin | Nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity | Aggressive IV hydration |

**Shared toxicities:** Bone marrow suppression, nausea, alopecia, mucositis, gonadal toxicity.

**Febrile neutropenia (ANC < 500 + fever ≥ 38°C):** Emergency — blood cultures then IV antibiotics within 1 hour.

**Vesicant extravasation:** STOP infusion; aspirate; cold pack (most); antidote if available; document and photograph.

---

## Five rights + five more

| Original five | Additional five |
| --- | --- |
| Patient | Reason |
| Drug | Response |
| Dose | Documentation |
| Route | Education |
| Time | Refusal (right to refuse) |

---

## Drug schedules (India)

| Schedule | Drugs | Requirement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| H | Standard prescription drugs | Prescription register |
| H1 | Reserve antibiotics | Separate sales register |
| X | Opioids, psychotropics | Triplicate prescription |

---

## Pharmacovigilance

- **PvPI:** Pharmacovigilance Programme of India — IPC/CDSCO, Uppsala Monitoring Centre (VigiBase)
- Nurse reports: any suspected ADR; serious ADR within 15 days
- **Serious ADR:** Death / life-threatening / hospitalisation / disability / congenital anomaly

---

## Vitamins — deficiency diseases

| Vitamin | Deficiency |
| --- | --- |
| A | Night blindness → xerophthalmia |
| D | Rickets (children), osteomalacia (adults) |
| K | Haemorrhagic disease of newborn; raised PT |
| B1 (thiamine) | Beriberi; Wernicke's encephalopathy — give IV before glucose |
| B3 (niacin) | Pellagra (4 Ds: Dermatitis, Diarrhoea, Dementia, Death) |
| B6 (pyridoxine) | Peripheral neuropathy; give with isoniazid |
| B12 | Megaloblastic anaemia + SACD; pernicious anaemia → IM injections |
| Folic acid | NTDs (supplement pre-conception); megaloblastic anaemia |
| C | Scurvy (bleeding gums, perifollicular haemorrhages) |

---

**Exam reminder:** Pharmacology II = Section A (38 marks) of the combined Semester 4 paper. Classify drugs by mechanism, state adverse effects and contraindications, end every answer with nurse's responsibilities.

# Unit 1: Drugs for ear, nose, throat and eye disorders, and drugs acting on the urinary system

INC Units I and II (4 + 4 hours): antihistamines and topical drugs for the eye, ear, nose and mouth; the renin–angiotensin system, diuretics and antidiuretics, drugs that harm the kidney, urinary antiseptics, and acidifiers and alkalinisers used in urinary tract infection (UTI). For each drug group learn the action, uses, contraindications, interactions, side effects and the nurse's role.

## 1.1 How to write a drug study

The INC syllabus asks the same points for every group. Use this order in every long answer and in your clinical drug study book.

```text
DRUG STUDY FRAME
1 Group / class and examples
2 Composition or preparation (eye drop, ointment, mouthwash, tablet)
3 Mechanism of action
4 Indications (uses)
5 Contraindications and cautions
6 Drug interactions
7 Side effects and adverse effects
8 Nurse's responsibilities: before, during and after giving the drug
   (assess → give safely → monitor → teach → record)
```

Doses are not given in these notes. In the ward, always take the dose, strength and route from the written order and the hospital formulary, and check the "rights" of drug administration (right patient, drug, dose, route, time, documentation, and the patient's right to information and to refuse).

## 1.2 Antihistamines (H1 receptor blockers)

**Histamine** is released from mast cells in allergy. Through **H1 receptors** it causes itching, sneezing, runny nose, dilatation and leakiness of small vessels (wheal and flare), and bronchial constriction. Through **H2 receptors** it increases gastric acid (H2 blockers belong to the GI drugs of Pharmacology I).

**Mechanism.** H1 antihistamines occupy the H1 receptor and stop histamine from acting (more exactly, they act as inverse agonists). They prevent the allergic response better than they reverse one that has already developed.

| Generation | Examples | Key features |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First (older, sedating) | Chlorpheniramine (CPM), promethazine, diphenhydramine, pheniramine, hydroxyzine, cyproheptadine, dimenhydrinate | Cross into the brain → drowsiness; anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention); some also stop motion sickness and vomiting |
| Second (newer, less sedating) | Cetirizine, levocetirizine, loratadine, desloratadine, fexofenadine | Little entry into the brain, mostly once-daily, few anticholinergic effects |

**Uses**
- Allergic rhinitis (hay fever), allergic conjunctivitis, urticaria, itching, insect bites.
- Add-on in anaphylaxis (after adrenaline, never instead of it — see Unit 5).
- Motion sickness and vertigo (promethazine, dimenhydrinate, cinnarizine).
- Sedation and pre-anaesthetic use (promethazine), cough and cold mixtures.
- Cyproheptadine has been used as an appetite stimulant; this use needs medical advice.

**Side effects.** Sedation and poor attention (older drugs), dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, urinary retention, thickened secretions; excitement in young children; headache. Promethazine injection irritates tissues.

**Cautions.** Glaucoma (angle-closure), enlarged prostate, the elderly (confusion, falls), young children, people who drive or work with machines, pregnancy and breast-feeding (check with the prescriber).

**Interactions.** Alcohol, sleeping pills, opioids and other CNS depressants add to the drowsiness; other anticholinergic drugs add to dryness and retention.

**Nursing responsibilities**
- Ask about allergy history, glaucoma, prostate problems and driving or machine work.
- Give sedating antihistamines at bedtime where possible.
- Raise the cot sides / keep the call bell near for elderly patients; help with walking.
- Teach: avoid alcohol and driving after older antihistamines; sip water or suck sugar-free sweets for dry mouth.
- Observe for urinary retention in older men.

### Other drugs for the nose

| Group | Examples | Points for the nurse |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Nasal decongestants (alpha agonists) | Oxymetazoline, xylometazoline, phenylephrine; oral pseudoephedrine | Shrink swollen nasal mucosa by vasoconstriction. Use for a few days only: longer use causes **rebound congestion (rhinitis medicamentosa)**. Oral forms can raise BP — caution in hypertension and heart disease. |
| Intranasal corticosteroids | Fluticasone, budesonide, mometasone, beclomethasone | Best long-term control of allergic rhinitis; take daily; effect builds over days; occasional nose bleed and dryness. |
| Mast cell stabiliser | Sodium cromoglycate | Prevents release of histamine; used before exposure. |
| Saline drops or spray | Normal saline | Safe for infants; loosens crusts and mucus. |

**Instilling nose drops:** clear the nose by gentle blowing; tilt the head back (or lie with the head over the edge of the bed); insert the dropper just inside the nostril without touching it; stay in position for a few minutes so the drug spreads; clean the dropper. Rationale: avoiding contact keeps the dropper clean; the position lets the drop reach the mucosa rather than run down the throat.

## 1.3 Topical drugs for the eye

The INC syllabus names **chloramphenicol and gentamicin eye drops**. Learn these two well and know the other eye drug groups for MCQs.

### Chloramphenicol eye drops and ointment

- **Class:** broad-spectrum antibiotic, mainly bacteriostatic.
- **Action:** binds the 50S ribosomal subunit of bacteria and blocks protein synthesis.
- **Uses:** bacterial conjunctivitis, superficial eye infections, prevention of infection after minor eye injury or foreign body removal.
- **Side effects:** brief stinging, blurred vision after ointment. Very rarely, blood disorders have been linked even to eye use, so prolonged use is avoided and it is used with care in people with a past blood disorder.
- **Nursing:** check the expiry (the opened bottle is usually discarded after the period printed on it, often about four weeks); do not share bottles; teach hand-washing.

### Gentamicin eye drops

- **Class:** aminoglycoside antibiotic, bactericidal.
- **Action:** binds the 30S ribosomal subunit → misreading of the genetic code → faulty proteins → bacterial death.
- **Uses:** bacterial conjunctivitis, keratitis and blepharitis caused by Gram-negative organisms such as Pseudomonas.
- **Side effects:** burning, irritation, local allergy. Systemic effects (kidney and ear damage) do not occur with normal eye use but are important when gentamicin is injected.

### Other eye drugs

| Group | Examples | Use | Nursing point |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Other antibacterials | Ciprofloxacin, moxifloxacin, tobramycin | Conjunctivitis, corneal ulcer | Complete the prescribed course |
| Antivirals | Acyclovir eye ointment | Herpes simplex keratitis | Steroid drops must not be used in herpes keratitis |
| Antifungals | Natamycin | Fungal keratitis | Common after injury with plant matter |
| Mydriatics / cycloplegics | Atropine, homatropine, tropicamide, cyclopentolate; phenylephrine (mydriatic only) | Eye examination, refraction, iritis | Blurred vision and glare — patient must not drive; atropine effect lasts many days; caution in angle-closure glaucoma |
| Miotics | Pilocarpine | Glaucoma (angle-closure), reverse dilatation | Dim vision in poor light, brow ache |
| Anti-glaucoma drugs | Timolol (beta blocker), latanoprost (prostaglandin), dorzolamide (carbonic anhydrase inhibitor), brimonidine (alpha agonist); acetazolamide tablets | Lower intra-ocular pressure | Timolol can be absorbed and slow the heart or worsen asthma; latanoprost can darken the iris |
| Local anaesthetic drops | Proparacaine, tetracaine | Tonometry, removing foreign body | Protect the eye after use: blink reflex is lost; never give to the patient to take home |
| Corticosteroid drops | Prednisolone, dexamethasone | Allergic and post-operative inflammation | Only under an eye doctor: can raise eye pressure, cause cataract and worsen infection |
| Lubricants | Carboxymethylcellulose, hypromellose | Dry eye | Safe for frequent use |

### Instilling eye drops (steps with rationale)

1. Check the order, the eye (right, left or both) and the label. **Rationale:** wrong-eye errors are common.
2. Wash hands; clean the eyelids from the inner to the outer corner with a separate swab for each eye. **Rationale:** avoids carrying discharge into the tear duct or the other eye.
3. Ask the patient to look up; pull the lower lid down to form a pocket.
4. Hold the dropper about 1–2 cm above the eye and drop into the **lower conjunctival sac**, not onto the cornea. **Rationale:** the cornea is sensitive and the drop would make the patient blink it out.
5. Ask the patient to close the eye gently (not squeeze) and press the **inner corner (nasolacrimal duct)** for about a minute. **Rationale:** keeps the drug in the eye and reduces absorption into the body (important with timolol and atropine).
6. With two different drops, wait about 5 minutes between them; drops before ointment.
7. Do not let the tip touch the eye; record the drug, eye and time.

## 1.4 Topical drugs for the ear

### Soda glycerin ear drops

- **Composition:** sodium bicarbonate (soda) in glycerin and water.
- **Action:** the alkali softens and loosens hard wax; glycerin lubricates. It is a **ceruminolytic (wax softener)**.
- **Use:** impacted wax before syringing or suction, or to let wax come out by itself.
- **Side effects:** temporary fullness, mild irritation, sometimes giddiness if the drop is cold.
- **Contraindication:** perforated ear drum, ear discharge.

### Boric spirit ear drops

- **Composition:** boric acid dissolved in rectified spirit (alcohol).
- **Action:** mild antiseptic and antifungal (boric acid) plus a drying effect (spirit), which removes the moist conditions germs like.
- **Uses:** otitis externa, fungal infection of the ear canal (otomycosis), after swimming.
- **Side effects:** burning or stinging, especially on raw skin.
- **Contraindication:** perforated ear drum (it burns the middle ear), and not for infants or long-term use.

### Other ear preparations
- Antibiotic and antibiotic–steroid drops: ciprofloxacin, ofloxacin (ofloxacin is chosen when the drum may be perforated, because some aminoglycoside drops can harm the inner ear through a perforation).
- Antifungal: clotrimazole drops for otomycosis.
- Hydrogen peroxide and olive oil drops also soften wax.

### Instilling ear drops (steps with rationale)

1. Warm the bottle in the hand to body temperature. **Rationale:** cold drops stimulate the inner ear and cause giddiness and vomiting.
2. Patient lies on the side, affected ear up.
3. Straighten the ear canal: **adult — pull the pinna up and back; child under 3 years — pull it down and back.** **Rationale:** the canal of a young child is directed upward.
4. Instil along the wall of the canal, not directly on the drum.
5. Press the tragus gently; keep the position for a few minutes; a loose cotton plug may be placed if ordered.
6. Teach the patient not to put sticks, pins or oil into the ear without advice.

## 1.5 Drugs for the mouth and throat: chlorhexidine mouthwash

- **Class:** biguanide antiseptic.
- **Action:** the positively charged molecule binds the negatively charged bacterial cell wall, damages the membrane and causes leakage of cell contents. It also sticks to teeth and gums and keeps acting for hours (**substantivity**).
- **Uses:** gingivitis and plaque control, oral care of ill, unconscious and ventilated patients (part of bundles to reduce ventilator-associated pneumonia), mouth ulcers, after oral surgery, oral care in patients receiving cancer chemotherapy.
- **Side effects:** **brown staining of teeth and tongue**, altered taste, mild burning, rarely allergy.
- **Interaction:** ordinary toothpaste (anionic detergents) reduces its effect — leave a gap of about 30 minutes, or rinse well between them.
- **Nursing:** teach to rinse and spit, **not swallow**; avoid food and drink for a while after use so the drug stays on the teeth; in unconscious patients use a swab or toothbrush with suction, with the head turned to the side to prevent aspiration.

Other mouth and throat products: povidone-iodine gargle (sore throat; avoid in iodine allergy and thyroid disease), benzydamine (pain-relieving mouthwash for mucositis), clotrimazole troches and nystatin suspension (oral thrush), glycerin-based paints, warm saline gargles.

## 1.6 The renin–angiotensin system and drugs that act on it

```text
Fall in BP / fall in renal blood flow / low sodium
            ↓
Kidney (juxtaglomerular cells) releases RENIN
Angiotensinogen (liver) ──renin──► Angiotensin I
Angiotensin I ──ACE (lungs)──► ANGIOTENSIN II
            ↓
• Strong vasoconstriction → BP ↑
• Aldosterone release → Na+ and water kept, K+ lost
• Thirst and ADH release
• Long term: growth of heart and vessel walls (remodelling)

ACE also breaks down BRADYKININ (a vasodilator that causes cough).
```

| Group | Examples | Action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ACE inhibitors | Captopril, enalapril, lisinopril, ramipril | Block conversion of angiotensin I to II; bradykinin also builds up |
| Angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) | Losartan, telmisartan, olmesartan, valsartan | Block the AT1 receptor; no bradykinin build-up, so no cough |
| Direct renin inhibitor | Aliskiren | Blocks renin itself |
| Aldosterone antagonists | Spironolactone, eplerenone | Block the end of the chain (see diuretics) |

**Uses.** Hypertension, heart failure, after myocardial infarction, **diabetic kidney disease** (they reduce protein loss in urine and slow kidney damage).

**Adverse effects (remember "CAPTOPRIL")** — Cough (dry, persistent), Angioedema (swelling of lips, tongue, throat — stop the drug, emergency), Proteinuria (rare), Taste change, Orthostatic and first-dose hypotension, Pregnancy harm (contraindicated), Renal function worsens in bilateral renal artery stenosis, Increased potassium (hyperkalaemia), Leucopenia (rare, captopril). ARBs share most of these except the cough.

**Interactions.** Potassium supplements, salt substitutes and potassium-sparing diuretics → high potassium; NSAIDs reduce the BP-lowering effect and with diuretics can harm the kidney; lithium levels rise.

**Nursing responsibilities**
- Check BP lying and standing; give the first dose at bedtime or with the patient lying down; watch for dizziness.
- Check serum potassium and creatinine before and during treatment.
- Ask about pregnancy or plans for pregnancy; teach women to report pregnancy at once.
- Teach the patient to report dry cough, and to seek help at once for swelling of the face, lips or tongue.
- Avoid potassium-rich salt substitutes unless advised.

## 1.7 Diuretics

A diuretic increases the output of urine by increasing the excretion of sodium (natriuresis) and water. Where a diuretic acts in the nephron decides how strong it is.

```text
NEPHRON AND SITE OF ACTION
Glomerulus
   ↓
PCT  ← carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (acetazolamide); osmotic diuretics (mannitol) act here and in the loop
   ↓
Loop of Henle, thick ascending limb ← LOOP diuretics (furosemide) block Na+/K+/2Cl– carrier  — strongest
   ↓
DCT  ← THIAZIDES (hydrochlorothiazide) block Na+/Cl– carrier — moderate
   ↓
Collecting duct ← POTASSIUM-SPARING: spironolactone (blocks aldosterone), amiloride/triamterene (block Na+ channel) — weak
```

| Class | Examples | Main uses | Main adverse effects |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Loop (high-ceiling) | Furosemide, torsemide, bumetanide | Acute pulmonary oedema, oedema of heart, liver and kidney failure, hypercalcaemia | Low K+, Na+, Mg2+; dehydration and low BP; **ototoxicity** (ringing, deafness, especially with fast IV injection or with aminoglycosides); raised uric acid and sugar |
| Thiazide and thiazide-like | Hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone, indapamide, metolazone | Hypertension (first-line), mild oedema, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, calcium kidney stones | Low K+ and Na+, raised uric acid (gout), raised sugar and lipids; **calcium is kept** (high calcium) |
| Potassium-sparing — aldosterone antagonists | Spironolactone, eplerenone | Heart failure, liver cirrhosis with ascites, primary hyperaldosteronism; given with loop/thiazide to save K+ | **Hyperkalaemia**; spironolactone causes gynaecomastia and menstrual changes |
| Potassium-sparing — Na+ channel blockers | Amiloride, triamterene | With thiazides to prevent K+ loss | Hyperkalaemia |
| Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors | Acetazolamide | Glaucoma, altitude sickness, some epilepsy | Metabolic acidosis, tingling, kidney stones; weak diuretic |
| Osmotic | Mannitol (IV) | Raised intracranial pressure, raised eye pressure, to keep urine flowing | Expands blood volume first — can cause pulmonary oedema in heart failure; crystals form in cold, so warm and use an in-line filter |

**Important interactions.** Low potassium from loop or thiazide diuretics makes **digoxin toxicity** more likely; diuretics raise **lithium** levels; aminoglycosides plus loop diuretics → more ear and kidney damage; NSAIDs reduce the diuretic effect; potassium-sparing diuretics plus ACE inhibitors or K+ supplements → dangerous hyperkalaemia.

**Nursing responsibilities with diuretics**
1. **Before:** record weight, BP (lying and standing), pulse, intake–output, serum electrolytes, creatinine, blood sugar; note hearing.
2. **Timing:** give in the **morning** (or the second dose by early afternoon) so the patient is not up at night to pass urine — less sleep loss and fewer night-time falls.
3. **IV furosemide:** inject slowly as ordered; fast injection increases the risk of hearing damage.
4. **Monitor:** daily weight at the same time with the same clothes and scale (the best guide to fluid loss), intake–output chart, oedema, lung sounds, signs of low potassium (muscle weakness, cramps, irregular pulse) or high potassium with K-sparing drugs.
5. **Safety:** postural hypotension — rise slowly; keep a urinal or bedpan within reach.
6. **Teach:** potassium-rich foods (banana, orange, coconut water, tomato) with loop and thiazide diuretics unless on a K-sparing drug; report weakness, giddiness, ringing in the ears; diabetic patients to check sugar.

## 1.8 Antidiuretics

**Antidiuretic hormone (ADH, vasopressin)** from the posterior pituitary acts on **V2 receptors** in the collecting duct, inserting water channels (aquaporins) so water is reabsorbed and urine becomes concentrated. Through **V1 receptors** it constricts blood vessels.

| Drug | Action | Uses | Adverse effects and nursing |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Vasopressin | V1 + V2 | Bleeding oesophageal varices (vasoconstriction), vasodilatory shock, diabetes insipidus | Chest pain from coronary constriction, abdominal cramps, pallor; monitor ECG and BP |
| Desmopressin (DDAVP) | Mainly V2, long acting; given by nose, mouth or injection | **Central (cranial) diabetes insipidus**, bed-wetting (nocturnal enuresis) in children, haemophilia A and von Willebrand disease (raises factor VIII) | **Water retention and low sodium** (headache, confusion, fits). Restrict fluids in the evening for enuresis; daily weight and serum sodium |
| Thiazides | Paradoxically reduce urine volume | **Nephrogenic** diabetes insipidus | As above |

## 1.9 Drugs toxic to the kidney (nephrotoxic drugs)

The kidney receives a large share of the cardiac output and concentrates drugs in its tubules, so it is easily injured.

| Drug or group | How it damages |
| --- | --- |
| Aminoglycosides (gentamicin, amikacin) | Damage to tubule cells (acute tubular necrosis) |
| Amphotericin B | Tubular damage and narrowing of renal vessels |
| NSAIDs (ibuprofen, diclofenac) | Block prostaglandins that keep renal vessels open; interstitial nephritis |
| Vancomycin, polymyxins | Tubular damage, worse with aminoglycosides |
| Cisplatin, methotrexate (high dose) | Tubular damage; crystals in tubules |
| Cyclosporine, tacrolimus | Constriction of renal vessels |
| Iodinated contrast media | Contrast-associated kidney injury |
| ACE inhibitors / ARBs | Fall in filtration in bilateral renal artery stenosis or dehydration |
| Acyclovir (IV), sulphonamides | Crystals in tubules |
| Lithium | Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, chronic damage |

**Patients at higher risk:** the elderly, dehydrated patients, diabetes, existing kidney disease, heart failure, and those taking two or more of these drugs together (the "triple whammy" of diuretic + ACE inhibitor/ARB + NSAID is a well-known cause of kidney injury).

**Nursing:** keep the patient well hydrated unless fluid is restricted; record intake and output; check serum creatinine and urea; report urine output falling below the expected level; give nephrotoxic drugs exactly at the ordered times; help with drug level monitoring (blood samples at the stated time before or after a dose); point out to the prescriber if two kidney-toxic drugs are ordered together.

## 1.10 Urinary antiseptics and drugs for UTI

**Urinary antiseptics** reach useful levels only in urine, not in blood, so they treat or prevent lower UTI (cystitis) but not kidney infection or blood infection.

| Drug | Action and uses | Adverse effects | Nursing |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Nitrofurantoin** | Damages bacterial DNA and proteins; uncomplicated cystitis and long-term prevention | Nausea (take with food), **brown discoloration of urine (harmless)**, peripheral neuropathy, lung reactions with long use, haemolysis in G6PD deficiency | Avoid in poor kidney function (does not reach urine) and near term in pregnancy; tell the patient about urine colour |
| **Methenamine (hexamine)** | In **acid urine** breaks down to formaldehyde, which kills bacteria; long-term prevention | Gastric upset, bladder irritation | Needs acid urine — given with an acidifier; no use in an indwelling catheter (urine does not stay long enough) |
| **Nalidixic acid** | Older quinolone | GI upset, photosensitivity | Largely replaced by newer drugs |
| **Fosfomycin** | Blocks cell-wall synthesis; single-course treatment of cystitis | Diarrhoea | Dissolve the sachet in water |
| Systemic antibiotics used for UTI | Cotrimoxazole, fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, norfloxacin), cephalosporins (cefixime, ceftriaxone), amoxicillin–clavulanate, aminoglycosides | See Pharmacology I | Choose by culture report |
| Urinary analgesic | Phenazopyridine | Turns urine orange-red; relieves burning only, does not cure infection | Short use only |

### Acidifiers and alkalinisers of urine

| Group | Examples | Why used |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Urinary acidifiers** | Ammonium chloride, ascorbic acid (vitamin C), methionine | Keep the urine acid so methenamine works; acid urine also slows growth of some germs and dissolves phosphate stones |
| **Urinary alkalinisers** | **Potassium citrate, sodium citrate**, sodium bicarbonate | Relieve the burning of cystitis; prevent uric acid and cystine stones; keep sulphonamides dissolved so they do not crystallise; aminoglycosides and some other antibiotics work better in alkaline urine |

Cautions: alkalinisers containing potassium are avoided in kidney failure and with K-sparing diuretics (high potassium); sodium salts add to the salt load in heart failure and hypertension. An acidifier and an alkaliniser must never be given together.

**Nursing role in UTI**
1. Collect a **clean-catch midstream urine sample** (or from the catheter sampling port, never the bag) **before** the first antibiotic dose — the culture guides the choice of drug.
2. Encourage fluids (about 2–3 litres a day unless restricted) to flush the bladder.
3. Teach the patient to finish the full course even after symptoms settle; stopping early encourages resistance and relapse.
4. Teach prevention: perineal care front to back, passing urine after intercourse, not holding urine for long, catheter care.
5. Watch for fever, loin pain or rigors (spread to the kidney) and report.

## Remember

- Drug study order: class → composition → action → uses → contraindications → interactions → side effects → nurse's role.
- First-generation antihistamines sedate and dry; second-generation (cetirizine, fexofenadine) hardly sedate. In anaphylaxis, adrenaline first.
- Nasal decongestant sprays: a few days only — rebound congestion.
- Chloramphenicol: 50S, bacteriostatic. Gentamicin: 30S, bactericidal, Gram-negative.
- Eye drops into the lower conjunctival sac; press the inner canthus; 5 minutes between drops; steroid drops never in herpes keratitis.
- Ear drops warm; pull pinna up and back in adults, down and back in children under 3.
- Soda glycerin = wax softener; boric spirit = antiseptic and drying; both not in perforated drum.
- Chlorhexidine: stains teeth, do not swallow, keep away from toothpaste for ~30 minutes.
- ACE inhibitors: dry cough (bradykinin), angioedema, high K+, avoid in pregnancy.
- Loop diuretics strongest; ototoxic; low K+ raises digoxin toxicity. Thiazides keep calcium, raise uric acid. Spironolactone: high K+, gynaecomastia.
- Give diuretics in the morning; daily weight is the best guide.
- Desmopressin: V2, diabetes insipidus and bed-wetting; watch for low sodium.
- Nephrotoxic: aminoglycosides, amphotericin B, NSAIDs, cisplatin, contrast, cyclosporine.
- Nitrofurantoin turns urine brown; methenamine needs acid urine; citrates alkalinise.
- Urine culture before the first antibiotic dose.

# Unit 2: Analgesics, antipyretics, anaesthetics and medical gases

INC Unit III, first part (the unit has 10 hours in all): NSAIDs, antipyretics, opioids and other central analgesics; general anaesthesia (techniques and pre-anaesthetic medication); local anaesthetics; and medical gases — oxygen, nitrous oxide, carbon dioxide and others. The rest of Unit III (sedatives, psychiatric drugs, anticonvulsants and others) is in Unit 3 of these notes.

## 2.1 Pain and the groups of analgesics

**Pain** is an unpleasant sensory and emotional experience linked to actual or possible tissue damage. Injured tissue releases **prostaglandins, bradykinin and histamine**; prostaglandins make nerve endings more sensitive (hyperalgesia). Signals travel to the spinal cord and brain, where opioid receptors can block them.

| Group | Where it acts | Examples | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Non-opioid analgesics (NSAIDs, paracetamol) | Mainly at the site of injury by stopping prostaglandin formation | Aspirin, ibuprofen, diclofenac, paracetamol | Mild to moderate pain, inflammation, fever |
| Opioid analgesics | Brain and spinal cord (opioid receptors) | Morphine, fentanyl, tramadol | Moderate to severe pain |
| Adjuvant analgesics | Other mechanisms | Amitriptyline, gabapentin, pregabalin, carbamazepine, steroids | Nerve (neuropathic) pain, bone pain, swelling |

```text
WHO PAIN LADDER (for cancer and chronic pain)
Step 3  Severe pain    → strong opioid (morphine, fentanyl) ± non-opioid ± adjuvant
Step 2  Moderate pain  → weak opioid (tramadol, codeine) ± non-opioid ± adjuvant
Step 1  Mild pain      → non-opioid (paracetamol, NSAID) ± adjuvant
Principles: by mouth, by the clock, by the ladder, for the individual, with attention to detail
```

Nursing pain assessment comes first: site, character, severity on a 0–10 numerical scale or faces scale (children), what makes it better or worse, effect on sleep and movement. Reassess after every analgesic (about 30 minutes after IV, about an hour after oral).

## 2.2 Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)

**Mechanism.** NSAIDs block the **cyclo-oxygenase (COX)** enzyme that makes prostaglandins and thromboxane from arachidonic acid.

```text
Cell membrane phospholipids
        ↓ phospholipase A2   (blocked by corticosteroids)
Arachidonic acid
        ↓ COX-1 and COX-2     (blocked by NSAIDs)
Prostaglandins + thromboxane A2 + prostacyclin
COX-1 ("housekeeping"): protects stomach lining, keeps kidney blood flow, platelet aggregation
COX-2 (induced in inflammation): pain, fever, swelling
```

**Four actions:** analgesic, antipyretic, anti-inflammatory, and antiplatelet (mainly aspirin).

**Classification**

| Group | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| Non-selective COX inhibitors | Aspirin (irreversible), ibuprofen, naproxen, diclofenac, indomethacin, piroxicam, ketorolac, mefenamic acid |
| Preferential COX-2 inhibitors | Nimesulide, meloxicam, aceclofenac |
| Selective COX-2 inhibitors (coxibs) | Celecoxib, etoricoxib |
| Analgesic–antipyretic with poor anti-inflammatory action | Paracetamol (acetaminophen), metamizole |

**Uses.** Headache, toothache, dysmenorrhoea (mefenamic acid), musculoskeletal pain and sprains, arthritis (rheumatoid and osteoarthritis), gout, post-operative pain (ketorolac injection), fever, renal colic (diclofenac), and closure of patent ductus arteriosus in preterm babies (indomethacin, ibuprofen) under specialist care.

**Adverse effects**
- **Gastric irritation, peptic ulcer and GI bleeding** (loss of protective prostaglandins) — the most important.
- **Kidney**: salt and water retention, raised BP, kidney injury in dehydrated or elderly patients.
- **Bleeding tendency** (less platelet thromboxane).
- **Asthma** worsened in aspirin-sensitive people.
- **Heart**: selective COX-2 inhibitors and high-dose NSAIDs increase the risk of heart attack and stroke.
- **Pregnancy**: avoided in the third trimester — can close the baby's ductus arteriosus early and delay labour.
- Allergy, rashes; nimesulide carries a liver risk and is not used in children.

### Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid)
- Acetylates COX **irreversibly**; in platelets (which cannot make new enzyme) the effect lasts for their life span of about 7–10 days.
- Uses: low-dose aspirin as an **antiplatelet** to prevent heart attack and stroke; pain, fever and inflammation at higher doses (now less used).
- **Reye's syndrome:** aspirin given to children and teenagers with a viral illness (influenza, chickenpox) can cause serious liver and brain damage. **Aspirin is not given to children for fever.**
- Stop before surgery as advised by the surgeon (bleeding).
- Interactions: warfarin and other anticoagulants (bleeding), methotrexate (toxicity rises), other NSAIDs (stomach damage).

### Nursing responsibilities with NSAIDs
1. Ask about peptic ulcer, bleeding disorders, asthma, kidney disease, heart disease, pregnancy, and current anticoagulants.
2. Give **after food or with milk**; a proton pump inhibitor is often co-prescribed for long courses.
3. Watch for black stools, blood-stained vomit, epigastric pain, reduced urine, oedema and rising BP.
4. Do not combine two NSAIDs; check that "cold and pain" medicines the patient buys do not contain another NSAID.
5. **Dengue fever:** NSAIDs and aspirin are avoided because of bleeding risk; paracetamol is used for fever.

## 2.3 Antipyretics and paracetamol

**Fever** occurs when pyrogens (from infection or tissue damage) cause prostaglandin E2 to raise the "set point" of the heat-regulating centre in the hypothalamus. Antipyretics lower the set point back to normal; they do not lower a normal temperature.

### Paracetamol (acetaminophen)
- **Action:** weak COX inhibitor, acting mainly in the brain; little effect in inflamed tissue, so it is a good analgesic and antipyretic but **not anti-inflammatory**.
- **Advantages:** no stomach irritation, no effect on platelets, safe in asthma; preferred antipyretic in children, pregnancy and dengue.
- **Uses:** fever, headache, mild to moderate pain; part of multimodal post-operative analgesia (oral or IV).
- **Adverse effects:** rare at the right dose; rash. Taken above the safe daily limit, or in people with liver disease, heavy alcohol use or malnutrition, it can cause serious **liver damage**. N-acetylcysteine is its specific antidote (Unit 5).
- **Nursing:** count all paracetamol from every source (many cold remedies contain it); follow the minimum gap between doses on the order; record temperature before and about an hour after; combine with cooling measures.

**Nursing care in fever:** check temperature, pulse and respiration regularly; light clothing and a ventilated room; **tepid sponging** in high fever (not cold or ice water, which causes shivering and raises heat production); plenty of oral fluids; watch children for febrile fits; find and treat the cause.

## 2.4 Opioids and other central analgesics

**Opioid receptors:** mu (μ), kappa (κ), delta (δ). Most strong opioid effects — analgesia, euphoria, respiratory depression, constipation, dependence — are through **mu receptors**.

| Type | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| Natural (opium alkaloids) | Morphine, codeine |
| Semi-synthetic and synthetic agonists | Pethidine (meperidine), fentanyl, methadone, tramadol, tapentadol |
| Partial agonist | Buprenorphine |
| Mixed agonist–antagonists | Pentazocine, butorphanol, nalbuphine |
| Pure antagonists | **Naloxone** (reverses opioid effects; short-acting, by injection), **naltrexone** (oral; used in deaddiction, Unit 5) |

### Morphine — the prototype

| System | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| CNS | Strong analgesia, sedation, mood elevation (euphoria), suppression of cough centre, **respiratory depression** (main danger), stimulation of the chemoreceptor trigger zone → nausea and vomiting, **pin-point pupils (miosis)** |
| GI tract | Reduced movement → **constipation** (no tolerance develops to this); spasm of the sphincter of Oddi → biliary pain |
| Urinary | Urinary retention |
| CVS | Vasodilatation, postural hypotension; reduces preload — helps acute pulmonary oedema |
| Skin | Histamine release → itching, flushing; can trigger bronchospasm |
| Other | Raised intracranial pressure (from CO2 retention) |

**Uses:** severe acute pain (fractures, burns, myocardial infarction, post-operative), cancer pain, acute left ventricular failure with pulmonary oedema, pre-anaesthetic medication; codeine and dextromethorphan for dry cough; loperamide (opioid that stays in the gut) for diarrhoea.

**Contraindications and cautions:** head injury (masks pupils and consciousness, raises ICP), respiratory disease and acute asthma, liver failure, hypothyroidism, the elderly and infants (more sensitive), labour close to delivery (can depress the newborn's breathing), biliary colic.

**Tolerance and dependence:** with repeated use larger amounts are needed for the same effect, and stopping suddenly causes withdrawal (yawning, watering eyes, runny nose, gooseflesh, cramps, diarrhoea, restlessness). In cancer pain these are not a reason to withhold good pain relief; doses are reduced gradually rather than stopped suddenly. Opioids are **narcotic drugs under the NDPS Act, 1985**, so hospitals keep them in a double-locked cupboard with a register.

**Interactions:** alcohol, benzodiazepines, antihistamines and other sedatives add to respiratory depression; MAO inhibitors with pethidine can cause a dangerous reaction; tramadol with SSRIs can cause serotonin syndrome.

**Other opioids — key points**
- **Pethidine:** shorter acting; anticholinergic-like effects; its breakdown product can cause fits with repeated doses; not preferred for long use.
- **Fentanyl:** very potent and short-acting; used in anaesthesia, as skin patches in chronic cancer pain (heat over the patch increases absorption), and by infusion in ICU.
- **Tramadol:** weak mu agonist that also blocks reuptake of serotonin and noradrenaline; less respiratory depression; can cause fits and nausea.
- **Buprenorphine:** partial agonist with a ceiling effect; used for pain (patches) and in opioid substitution therapy.
- **Pentazocine:** can cause hallucinations and raise BP; can bring on withdrawal in people dependent on morphine.

### Nursing responsibilities with opioids
1. **Assess before giving:** pain score, **respiratory rate**, sedation level, BP and pulse, allergies, last dose time. If the respiratory rate is low or the patient is very drowsy, **withhold and inform the doctor** according to the ward protocol.
2. Check the order, then **count and record in the narcotic register with a second nurse as witness**; sign for every ampoule, including wasted portions.
3. After giving: monitor respiration and sedation regularly (especially after the first dose and in the first hours after IV use); keep **naloxone and an Ambu bag** at hand.
4. Prevent constipation from the start: fluids, fibre, a laxative as ordered.
5. Watch urine output and bladder distension; nausea (antiemetic as ordered).
6. Safety: raise side rails, help with walking (postural hypotension, drowsiness).
7. Patient-controlled analgesia (PCA): teach that only the patient presses the button, not relatives.
8. Teach patients going home: no alcohol or sleeping pills alongside, no driving while drowsy, keep the medicine locked away from children, return unused stock to the pharmacy.

### Adjuvant analgesics
Amitriptyline (tricyclic antidepressant), gabapentin and pregabalin (diabetic neuropathy, post-herpetic neuralgia), **carbamazepine (drug of choice in trigeminal neuralgia)**, corticosteroids (raised ICP, nerve compression), bisphosphonates (bone pain), and drugs for migraine (triptans for attacks; propranolol, flunarizine for prevention).

## 2.5 General anaesthesia

**General anaesthesia (GA)** is a reversible state of loss of consciousness with **analgesia, amnesia, muscle relaxation and loss of reflexes**, produced by drugs so that surgery can be done without pain or awareness.

### Stages of anaesthesia (Guedel's stages, seen best with ether)

| Stage | Name | Features |
| --- | --- | --- |
| I | Stage of analgesia | From start of induction to loss of consciousness; pain is reduced, patient still conscious |
| II | Stage of delirium (excitement) | Unconscious but restless, irregular breathing, vomiting possible — modern IV induction passes through it quickly |
| III | Stage of surgical anaesthesia | Regular breathing, muscle relaxation, eye movements cease; divided into four planes; surgery done in plane 2–3 |
| IV | Medullary paralysis | Failure of breathing and circulation — must never be reached |

### Techniques of GA
- **Induction:** usually by an IV agent (rapid and pleasant), or by inhaled gas in children who fear needles.
- **Maintenance:** inhaled agent or continuous IV infusion (total intravenous anaesthesia, TIVA).
- **Airway:** face mask, laryngeal mask airway, or endotracheal intubation (needs a muscle relaxant).
- **Balanced anaesthesia:** a combination of drugs, each doing one job — an IV inducer, an opioid for analgesia, a muscle relaxant, an inhaled agent for maintenance — so that each drug is used in a smaller amount with fewer side effects.
- **Recovery:** stopping the agents, reversal of muscle relaxant (neostigmine with glycopyrrolate, or sugammadex), extubation, and care in the post-anaesthesia care unit.

### IV anaesthetics

| Drug | Features | Points |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Thiopentone sodium | Ultra-short barbiturate; unconsciousness within one arm-brain circulation time; wakes quickly by **redistribution** from brain to muscle and fat | Extravasation or arterial injection is very irritant; can cause laryngospasm |
| Propofol | Rapid smooth induction and clear-headed recovery; also antiemetic | Pain on injection, fall in BP; preferred for day-care surgery; milky emulsion — strict asepsis |
| Ketamine | **Dissociative anaesthesia** — patient appears awake but feels no pain; good analgesia; raises BP and heart rate; relaxes bronchi | Emergence reactions (vivid dreams, hallucinations) — recover in a quiet room; useful in shock, asthma, burns dressings and children |
| Etomidate | Keeps heart and BP stable | Suppresses adrenal steroid production |
| Midazolam | Benzodiazepine; sedation and amnesia | Used for sedation in procedures and as premedication |

### Inhalational anaesthetics

| Agent | Points |
| --- | --- |
| Nitrous oxide | Weak anaesthetic, good analgesic; used as a carrier gas (see 2.7) |
| Sevoflurane | Pleasant smell, fast smooth induction — choice for inhaled induction in children |
| Isoflurane | Common maintenance agent; pungent |
| Desflurane | Very rapid recovery; irritant to airways |
| Halothane | Older; can sensitise the heart to adrenaline (arrhythmias) and rarely causes hepatitis |

**Malignant hyperthermia:** a rare inherited reaction to volatile anaesthetics and succinylcholine — rapid rise in temperature, muscle rigidity, high CO2. Treated with **dantrolene**, stopping the trigger, and cooling.

### Pre-anaesthetic medication

**Aims:** relieve anxiety, provide amnesia and analgesia, reduce secretions and vagal reflexes, prevent nausea and vomiting, reduce the risk of acid aspiration, and make induction smooth.

| Aim | Drugs |
| --- | --- |
| Anxiety relief, sedation, amnesia | Benzodiazepines — midazolam, diazepam, lorazepam |
| Analgesia | Opioids — fentanyl, morphine |
| Reduce secretions; prevent bradycardia from vagal reflexes | Anticholinergics — **glycopyrrolate**, atropine |
| Prevent nausea and vomiting | Ondansetron, metoclopramide, dexamethasone |
| Reduce gastric acid and volume (prevent aspiration pneumonitis — Mendelson's syndrome) | H2 blockers (famotidine), proton pump inhibitors (pantoprazole), metoclopramide, oral sodium citrate before caesarean section |

**Nurse's role before anaesthesia:** confirm written informed consent; nil by mouth as ordered (usually solids for several hours and clear fluids for a shorter time — follow the hospital policy); remove dentures, jewellery, nail polish and make-up; ask the patient to pass urine; record vital signs, weight and allergies; give premedication exactly at the ordered time; after a sedative premedication, **the patient stays in bed with side rails up** and does not sign any further documents.

**Nurse's role after GA:** maintain the airway (lateral position until reflexes return), monitor oxygen saturation, pulse, BP and level of consciousness; watch for nausea, shivering, pain and bleeding; do not give oral fluids until swallowing and cough reflexes are back.

## 2.6 Local anaesthetics

**Definition:** drugs that, applied locally to nerve tissue, reversibly block nerve conduction, causing loss of sensation in a limited area without loss of consciousness.

**Mechanism:** they enter the nerve fibre and **block voltage-gated sodium channels** from inside, so an action potential cannot be generated. Small, thin fibres are blocked first: **pain → temperature → touch → pressure → motor**; recovery is in the reverse order.

| Type | Examples | Points |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Esters** | Procaine, chloroprocaine, tetracaine, benzocaine | Broken down by plasma cholinesterase; short-acting; more allergy |
| **Amides** | **Lignocaine (lidocaine)**, bupivacaine, ropivacaine, prilocaine | Broken down in the liver; allergy rare. Trick: amides have an extra "i" before "-caine" |

- **Lignocaine:** quick and medium-acting; surface, infiltration, nerve blocks; also an antiarrhythmic (IV).
- **Bupivacaine:** long-acting; spinal and epidural anaesthesia; more harmful to the heart if it reaches the blood.
- **Ropivacaine:** long-acting, less cardiotoxic, less motor block — good for labour epidurals.
- **EMLA cream** (lignocaine + prilocaine): numbs skin before cannulation in children (apply under a dressing for the time stated).

**Adrenaline with local anaesthetic:** constricts vessels so the drug stays longer at the site, lasts longer, absorbs less into blood and causes less bleeding. **Never in areas supplied by end arteries** — fingers, toes, penis, ear lobe, tip of nose — because gangrene can result. Avoid in hypertension and heart disease.

**Techniques:** surface (topical) anaesthesia, infiltration, field block, nerve block, **spinal (subarachnoid) anaesthesia**, **epidural anaesthesia** (lumbar for labour and surgery; caudal in children), and IV regional anaesthesia (Bier's block).

**Adverse effects** when too much reaches the blood: numbness of tongue and lips, metallic taste, ringing in the ears, dizziness, muscle twitching, convulsions; fall in BP, slow heart rate, arrhythmias. Allergy (mainly esters).

**Spinal anaesthesia complications and nursing:** fall in BP (sympathetic block — IV fluids and vasopressor as ordered; monitor BP closely); slow heart rate; nausea; **post-dural puncture headache** (worse on sitting up — rest, fluids, analgesics, report); urinary retention; high block causing breathing difficulty.

**Nursing responsibilities with local anaesthetics**
- Ask about allergy to "caine" drugs and earlier reactions.
- Aspiration before injection is done by the operator to avoid injecting into a vessel; keep resuscitation drugs and equipment ready.
- Protect the numb part from injury (burns from hot bottles, pressure); after throat spray, **nothing by mouth until the gag reflex returns** (aspiration risk).
- Record when sensation and movement return.

## 2.7 Medical gases

### Oxygen
**Uses:** hypoxaemia from any cause — pneumonia, COPD exacerbation, heart failure, shock, cardiac arrest, carbon monoxide poisoning, anaesthesia and recovery, newborn resuscitation (as guided by saturation).

| Device | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| Nasal cannula | Low flow; comfortable, patient can eat and talk |
| Simple face mask | Moderate concentration |
| Venturi mask | Delivers a fixed, known concentration — preferred in COPD |
| Non-rebreathing mask with reservoir bag | High concentration in emergencies |
| High-flow nasal oxygen, CPAP, ventilators | ICU use |

**Hazards of oxygen therapy**
- **Fire:** oxygen supports burning — no smoking, no naked flames, no oil or grease on fittings, no woollen or synthetic blankets that make sparks; display "No smoking" signs.
- **CO2 narcosis in chronic COPD:** some patients depend on low oxygen to drive breathing; uncontrolled high oxygen can make breathing slow and CO2 rise. Give controlled oxygen to the **target saturation set by the doctor** (commonly lower in COPD than in other patients).
- **Oxygen toxicity of the lungs** with high concentrations for long periods; **absorption collapse** of alveoli.
- **Retinopathy of prematurity** in preterm babies — strict saturation targets in NICU.
- **Drying of mucosa** — humidify at higher flows; oral and nasal care.

### Nitrous oxide (N2O, "laughing gas")
- Sweet-smelling, non-irritant; **good analgesic, weak anaesthetic**; quick onset and offset.
- Uses: carrier gas with other anaesthetics; **Entonox (50% N2O + 50% O2)** for pain relief in labour, dressings and ambulances.
- **Diffusion hypoxia:** at the end of anaesthesia N2O floods out into the alveoli and dilutes oxygen — give 100% oxygen for a few minutes.
- Enters closed air spaces and expands them — avoid in pneumothorax, bowel obstruction, middle-ear surgery and after some eye surgeries using gas bubbles.
- Long or repeated exposure interferes with vitamin B12 → bone marrow and nerve damage.

### Carbon dioxide (CO2)
- Stimulates breathing (through chemoreceptors) and dilates cerebral vessels.
- Uses: **insufflation of the abdomen in laparoscopy**; cryotherapy (as solid "dry ice" or liquid CO2) for warts and cervical lesions; mixed with oxygen in some respiratory and anaesthesia uses.
- After laparoscopy, CO2 under the diaphragm causes **shoulder-tip pain**.
- Excess CO2 (hypercapnia) causes headache, flushing, confusion and acidosis.

### Other medical gases
- **Medical air:** for ventilators and to drive nebulisers.
- **Helium–oxygen (heliox):** low density, eases breathing past a narrowed airway.
- **Nitric oxide (inhaled):** relaxes pulmonary vessels in newborns with persistent pulmonary hypertension.
- **Ethylene oxide:** a gas used for sterilising heat-sensitive equipment, not for patients.

### Cylinder safety (nurse's responsibility)
- Read the **label** on the cylinder; colour codes (oxygen commonly black body with white shoulder, nitrous oxide blue, carbon dioxide grey) help, but the label is what you rely on.
- Store upright, chained or in a trolley, in a cool, ventilated place away from heat and flames.
- Open the valve slowly; check the pressure gauge and the flow meter; never use oil or grease; replace a near-empty cylinder in time.
- Use pin-index connections so that the wrong gas cannot be fitted.

## Remember

- NSAIDs block COX → less prostaglandin → analgesic, antipyretic, anti-inflammatory (± antiplatelet).
- Main NSAID dangers: stomach ulcer and bleeding, kidney injury, asthma, third-trimester pregnancy. Give after food.
- Aspirin: irreversible COX block, antiplatelet for the platelet's life; Reye's syndrome — not for children with viral fever.
- Paracetamol: no stomach or platelet effect; liver damage when the safe limit is exceeded; antidote N-acetylcysteine. Use in dengue fever.
- Morphine: mu agonist; respiratory depression, miosis, constipation, retention, itching, vomiting. Check respiratory rate first; naloxone reverses.
- Opioids are controlled under the NDPS Act: locked cupboard, register, witness.
- WHO ladder: by mouth, by the clock, by the ladder.
- GA = unconsciousness + analgesia + amnesia + relaxation; balanced anaesthesia uses several drugs.
- Thiopentone wakes by redistribution; propofol for day surgery; ketamine dissociative with emergence reactions; sevoflurane for children; dantrolene for malignant hyperthermia.
- Premedication: midazolam, fentanyl, glycopyrrolate, ondansetron, H2 blocker/PPI.
- Local anaesthetics block Na+ channels; pain fibres first; no adrenaline in fingers, toes, penis, ear, nose.
- Spinal anaesthesia: watch BP, headache, retention.
- Oxygen: fire hazard; controlled oxygen in COPD; ROP in preterms; humidify.
- N2O: analgesic; Entonox for labour; diffusion hypoxia — give 100% O2 at the end.
- CO2: laparoscopy insufflation (shoulder-tip pain), cryotherapy.

# Unit 3: Sedatives, muscle relaxants, psychiatric drugs, anticonvulsants and other CNS drugs

This is the second half of the large INC Unit III (drugs acting on the nervous system). Unit 2 covered pain, anaesthesia and gases; this unit covers drugs that calm or steady the brain and the muscles: hypnotics and sedatives, skeletal muscle relaxants, antipsychotics and mood stabilisers, antidepressants, antianxiety drugs, anticonvulsants, drugs for brain-wasting (neurodegenerative) disorders, stimulants, and the handling of alcohol and methyl-alcohol poisoning. For each group learn the action, uses, main adverse effects and the nurse's role. No doses are given; always take dose, strength and route from the written order.

## 3.1 Hypnotics and sedatives

- A **sedative** calms and reduces anxiety and activity.
- A **hypnotic** produces drowsiness and sleep.
The same drug is often a sedative in a small amount and a hypnotic in a larger one, so the two are studied together.

### Benzodiazepines (the main group)

**Action.** They attach to a site on the **GABA-A receptor** and make the brain's main calming transmitter, **GABA**, work better (more chloride enters the neuron, so it is harder to fire). They do not open the channel by themselves, which is why they are much safer in overdose than the older barbiturates.

| Short / intermediate acting | Long acting |
| --- | --- |
| Alprazolam, lorazepam, oxazepam, temazepam, midazolam | Diazepam, chlordiazepoxide, clonazepam, nitrazepam |

**Five actions ("the five A's")** — Anxiolytic (anti-anxiety), Anticonvulsant, Amnesic (loss of memory for events during the drug), muscle relaxant, and sedative-hypnotic.

**Uses.** Anxiety, short-term insomnia, status epilepticus and fits (lorazepam, diazepam, midazolam), alcohol withdrawal (chlordiazepoxide, diazepam), premedication and sedation for procedures (midazolam), muscle spasm.

**Adverse effects.** Drowsiness, poor coordination and memory, falls in the elderly, slurred speech; **tolerance and dependence** with long use; rebound anxiety and insomnia on stopping; breathing can be depressed when combined with opioids or alcohol.

**Antidote.** **Flumazenil** reverses benzodiazepines (used with care — it can cause fits in a dependent patient).

### Other hypnotics and sedatives

| Group | Examples | Key points |
| --- | --- | --- |
| "Z-drugs" (non-benzodiazepine) | Zolpidem, zopiclone, eszopiclone | Act at the same receptor; for short-term insomnia; sleep-walking and next-day drowsiness possible |
| Barbiturates (old) | Phenobarbitone, thiopentone | **Open** the chloride channel directly → dangerous in overdose (coma, stopped breathing), strong enzyme inducers, high dependence; now mostly only phenobarbitone (epilepsy) and thiopentone (anaesthesia) |
| Melatonin receptor type | Melatonin, ramelteon | Help the sleep–wake rhythm; mild |
| Sedating antihistamine | Diphenhydramine, promethazine | Occasional use for sleep (Unit 1) |

**Nursing responsibilities (sedatives and hypnotics)**
- Assess sleep pattern and the reason for sleeplessness; try non-drug measures first (quiet, dark, no caffeine late, a fixed routine).
- Give a hypnotic at bedtime; raise the cot sides and keep the call bell within reach; help the patient to the toilet to prevent falls.
- Warn against alcohol and against driving or working with machines.
- Teach that these drugs are for short-term use and must not be stopped suddenly after long use (withdrawal fits, severe anxiety).
- Count and store controlled sedatives as the law and hospital policy require.

## 3.2 Skeletal muscle relaxants

These relax voluntary (skeletal) muscle. They are of two broad kinds.

```text
SKELETAL MUSCLE RELAXANTS
├─ Centrally acting (reduce spasm from the brain/cord)
│    Baclofen, tizanidine, diazepam, chlorzoxazone, methocarbamol
│    Use: muscle spasm, spasticity in cerebral palsy, multiple sclerosis, stroke, back pain
│
└─ Peripherally acting = NEUROMUSCULAR BLOCKERS (act at the end-plate)
     ├─ Non-depolarising (compete with acetylcholine): vecuronium, rocuronium,
     │    atracurium, pancuronium → reversed by neostigmine (+ atropine/glycopyrrolate)
     └─ Depolarising (over-stimulate then block): succinylcholine (suxamethonium)
          → short action; NOT reversed by neostigmine
```

**Neuromuscular blockers** are used in the operation theatre and ICU to relax muscle for surgery, intubation and ventilation. They **do not relieve pain and do not cause sleep** — the patient must also receive an anaesthetic and an analgesic, or they will be awake and paralysed. Breathing stops, so ventilation is essential.

- **Succinylcholine:** very fast and short; used for rapid intubation. Can cause muscle pains, a rise in potassium (dangerous in burns and crush injury), and is a trigger of **malignant hyperthermia** (treated with dantrolene).
- **Dantrolene** acts inside the muscle cell (blocks calcium release) and is used for malignant hyperthermia and severe spasticity.

**Nursing responsibilities**
- Centrally acting relaxants cause drowsiness and low BP — the same fall and driving precautions as for sedatives; do not stop baclofen suddenly (rebound spasticity, fever).
- For neuromuscular blockers: these are theatre/ICU drugs; ensure airway, oxygen, ventilation and monitoring are ready; keep the reversal drug and resuscitation equipment at hand; **a paralysed patient may still feel and hear** — give sedation and explain, and protect the eyes and pressure areas.

## 3.3 Antipsychotics (neuroleptics) and mood stabilisers

Used for schizophrenia, mania, severe agitation and, in small amounts, for severe nausea and hiccups.

**Action.** They block **dopamine (D2) receptors** in the brain. Newer ones also block serotonin receptors.

| Type | Examples | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Typical (first generation) | Chlorpromazine, haloperidol, fluphenazine, trifluoperazine | Strong on positive symptoms (hallucinations, delusions); more movement side effects |
| Atypical (second generation) | Olanzapine, risperidone, quetiapine, clozapine, aripiprazole | Fewer movement effects; help negative symptoms; more weight gain, raised sugar and lipids |

**Adverse effects**
- **Extrapyramidal side effects (EPS):** drug-induced parkinsonism (tremor, stiffness), acute dystonia (muscle spasm of the neck/eyes), akathisia (restlessness), and **tardive dyskinesia** (late, often lasting involuntary movements of the mouth and tongue). More common with typical drugs.
- **Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS):** rare, dangerous — high fever, severe muscle rigidity, confusion, unstable BP and pulse. **Stop the drug, cool the patient, report at once.**
- Sedation, low BP on standing, dry mouth and constipation (anticholinergic), weight gain, raised blood sugar and lipids, raised prolactin (breast changes, menstrual upset), prolonged QT on the ECG.
- **Clozapine** can cause a dangerous fall in white cells (**agranulocytosis**) — regular blood counts are required.

**Mood stabilisers**
- **Lithium** for bipolar disorder (mania and prevention). It has a **narrow safety margin**, so blood levels are checked. Early toxicity: tremor, nausea, diarrhoea, drowsiness; severe toxicity: coarse tremor, confusion, slurred speech, fits. Dehydration, low salt and diuretics and NSAIDs raise the level. Long use affects the thyroid and kidney. Teach steady salt and water intake and to report vomiting, diarrhoea or fever.
- **Valproate, carbamazepine and lamotrigine** (also antiepileptics, see 3.6) are used as mood stabilisers.

**Nursing responsibilities**
- Watch for and report movement disorders, fever with rigidity (NMS), and in clozapine patients a sore throat or fever (infection).
- Check BP (especially on standing), weight, blood sugar and, where ordered, the ECG and drug levels.
- Rise slowly, sip water for dry mouth, use sunscreen (photosensitivity with chlorpromazine).
- Depot (long-acting injection) forms help patients who forget tablets; give deep IM and rotate sites.
- Support the patient and family, encourage adherence, and watch mood and suicide risk.

## 3.4 Antidepressants

**Action.** Most increase the brain levels of **serotonin and/or noradrenaline**. The mood lifts slowly over **2–4 weeks**, although side effects start at once — an important teaching point.

| Group | Examples | Key points |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **SSRIs** (first choice) | Fluoxetine, sertraline, escitalopram, paroxetine | Block serotonin reuptake; nausea, headache, sexual problems, early restlessness; safer in overdose |
| **SNRIs** | Venlafaxine, duloxetine | Serotonin + noradrenaline; also used for nerve pain |
| **Tricyclics (TCAs)** | Amitriptyline, imipramine, nortriptyline | Effective but many anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, retention, constipation), low BP, **heart rhythm danger in overdose** |
| **MAO inhibitors** | Phenelzine, tranylcypromine; moclobemide (reversible) | Rarely used; a serious **tyramine ("cheese") reaction** — a dangerous rise in BP with aged cheese, red wine, pickled and fermented foods |
| Atypical / others | Mirtazapine, bupropion, trazodone | Mirtazapine aids sleep and appetite; bupropion also helps smoking cessation |

**Serotonin syndrome** — too much serotonin from combining serotonergic drugs: agitation, fever, sweating, tremor, fast pulse, rigidity. Stop the drugs and report.

**Nursing responsibilities**
- Teach that the mood effect takes a few weeks; do not stop early; do not stop suddenly (discontinuation symptoms).
- **Watch suicide risk closely in the first weeks**, especially in young people — energy may return before the mood lifts.
- Do not combine serotonergic drugs without advice; on an MAOI, teach the food and drug restrictions.
- For TCAs, watch for constipation, retention and postural fall; keep only small supplies with at-risk patients.

## 3.5 Antianxiety drugs

- **Benzodiazepines** (see 3.1) — fast relief, but for short-term use because of dependence.
- **SSRIs/SNRIs** — the mainstay for long-term anxiety disorders.
- **Buspirone** — a non-sedating anti-anxiety drug; works slowly, no dependence.
- **Beta-blockers** (propranolol) — reduce the physical signs of anxiety (racing heart, tremor), useful for performance anxiety.
- **Hydroxyzine** — a sedating antihistamine used for anxiety.

## 3.6 Anticonvulsants (antiepileptic drugs)

Epilepsy is repeated fits from sudden excessive electrical discharge in the brain. These drugs **reduce that excess firing** (block sodium or calcium channels, or boost GABA).

| Drug | Useful in | Points for the nurse |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Phenytoin** | Generalised tonic–clonic and focal seizures, status epilepticus | Gum overgrowth, hair growth, acne, unsteadiness; many interactions (enzyme inducer); give IV slowly with saline (not glucose) and watch the ECG |
| **Carbamazepine** | Focal seizures, trigeminal neuralgia, bipolar | Dizziness, low sodium, blood and skin reactions; serious rash risk |
| **Sodium valproate** | Most seizure types, absence, mania | Weight gain, hair loss, tremor, liver and pancreas injury; **avoid in pregnancy — causes birth defects** |
| **Phenobarbitone** | Fits, neonatal seizures | Sedation, dependence |
| **Benzodiazepines** | Status epilepticus (lorazepam/diazepam), absence (clonazepam) | First-line to stop a fit |
| **Ethosuximide** | Absence (petit mal) only | Nausea |
| Newer drugs | Levetiracetam, lamotrigine, gabapentin, topiramate, oxcarbazepine | Fewer interactions; lamotrigine — serious rash if increased too fast; levetiracetam — mood changes |

**Status epilepticus** is a fit lasting a long time or repeated fits without recovery in between — an emergency. Protect the airway, give oxygen, turn to the side, do not force anything into the mouth, and give the ordered IV benzodiazepine, then a longer-acting drug such as phenytoin.

**Nursing responsibilities**
- **Never stop an antiepileptic suddenly** — this can trigger status epilepticus; teach steady, regular dosing.
- Safety during a fit: protect the head, loosen tight clothes, turn to the side when able, time the fit, do not restrain or put anything in the mouth; stay and record what happened.
- Teach: carry an identity card, take drugs at the same time daily, avoid triggers (missed sleep, alcohol, flashing lights), and report any rash at once.
- **Pregnancy:** women of childbearing age need advice before conceiving; folic acid is given and valproate avoided; report pregnancy early.
- Phenytoin: teach good gum care and dental visits.

## 3.7 Drugs for neurodegenerative and miscellaneous disorders

**Parkinson's disease** — loss of dopamine neurons causes tremor, rigidity and slow movement. Drugs restore dopamine or reduce the opposing acetylcholine.

| Group | Examples | Points |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dopamine precursor | **Levodopa + carbidopa** | Most effective; carbidopa stops breakdown outside the brain so less nausea; "wearing-off" and involuntary movements after years; low BP; dark sweat/urine |
| Dopamine agonists | Bromocriptine, ropinirole, pramipexole | Nausea, sleepiness, impulse-control problems |
| MAO-B / COMT inhibitors | Selegiline, entacapone | Prolong dopamine action |
| Anticholinergics | Trihexyphenidyl, benztropine | Help tremor; dry mouth, retention |
| Others | Amantadine | Mild benefit |

**Alzheimer's disease / dementia** — **cholinesterase inhibitors** (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) raise acetylcholine; **memantine** (an NMDA blocker) for moderate–severe disease. They slow symptoms but do not cure. Side effects: nausea, slow pulse, diarrhoea.

**Nursing:** give levodopa on time (fixed schedule matters for mobility); it can be reduced by protein-rich meals and vitamin B6; watch for falls, low BP and confusion; support the carer; keep a safe, calm environment for people with dementia.

## 3.8 Central stimulants, ethyl alcohol and methyl-alcohol poisoning

**Central stimulants** speed up brain activity.

| Drug / class | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Caffeine | Mild stimulant; apnoea of prematurity |
| Methylphenidate, atomoxetine | Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) |
| Modafinil | Excessive daytime sleepiness/narcolepsy |
| Doxapram | Respiratory stimulant (rarely) |
| Amphetamines | Mostly drugs of abuse |

**Ethyl alcohol (ethanol)** is a CNS **depressant**, not a stimulant (the early "lively" feeling comes from loss of self-control). It is used medically as an antiseptic skin preparation, and as the **antidote for methanol and ethylene-glycol poisoning**.

**Methyl alcohol (methanol) poisoning** — methanol itself is not very harmful, but the body changes it into **formic acid**, which causes a dangerous acid build-up (metabolic acidosis), **blindness** (damage to the optic nerve) and death. It occurs with illicit/spurious liquor.
- Treatment: **fomepizole** or **ethanol** (both block the enzyme that makes formic acid, so methanol can be removed unchanged), **sodium bicarbonate** for the acidosis, **folinic acid**, and **haemodialysis** to remove methanol and formate.
- Nursing: support breathing and circulation, protect against aspiration, monitor vision and acid–base status, give the ordered antidote and prepare for dialysis, and teach the community about the danger of illicit liquor.

## Remember

- Benzodiazepines enhance GABA (safer); barbiturates open the chloride channel (dangerous overdose). Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines.
- Hypnotics at bedtime; fall precautions; short-term use; do not stop suddenly after long use.
- Neuromuscular blockers paralyse but give no sleep or pain relief — always need ventilation, sedation and analgesia; succinylcholine → high K+, malignant hyperthermia (dantrolene).
- Antipsychotics block dopamine → EPS, tardive dyskinesia, NMS (fever + rigidity, emergency); clozapine → agranulocytosis (blood counts).
- Lithium: narrow margin, check levels, steady salt and water; diuretics/NSAIDs/dehydration raise it.
- Antidepressants act over 2–4 weeks; watch suicide risk early; SSRIs first-line; MAOIs → tyramine reaction; serotonin syndrome if combined.
- Antiepileptics: never stop suddenly; valproate avoided in pregnancy; protect the patient during a fit, never restrain or put things in the mouth; status epilepticus — IV benzodiazepine first.
- Levodopa + carbidopa for Parkinson's — give on time; cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil) for Alzheimer's.
- Ethanol is a depressant and the antidote for methanol poisoning; methanol → formic acid → acidosis and blindness.
